en: It should be understood that rain, however, arises solely from its own causes. Likewise, auspiciousness [leads] to the destruction of obstacles.

Regarding its being a cause: "as one for whom the absence of obstacles is self-established" means as one for whom there is the absolute non-existence of obstacles. Now, one might ask: how can there even be an engagement with something fruitless?
To this he says: "due to the suspicion of obstacles. It is simply the cognition of an obstacle, common to both doubt and certainty [that motivates action].

The sense is that it is "that which initiates" [the work]. This is because of its performance, that is, because of the performance of an auspicious rite (*maṅgalācaraṇa*). Now, one might object that the performance of an auspicious rite is itself unestablished when there is doubt regarding obstacles; to this he says: "In that very way. The phrase "from the practice of the learned" (*śiṣṭācārāt*) implies that the auspicious rite [is established] by way of the relation of objective domain (*viṣayatā-sambandha*). Now, one might object: [...text missing... The sense is that it is "that which initiates" [the work]. This is because of its performance, that is, because of the performance of an auspicious rite (*maṅgalācaraṇa*). Now, one might object that the performance of an auspicious rite is itself unestablished when there is doubt regarding obstacles; to this he says: "In that very way. The phrase "from the practice of the learned" (*śiṣṭācārāt*) implies that the auspicious rite [is established] by way of the relation of objective domain (*viṣayatā-sambandha*). Now, one might object:

If it is argued that the causal efficacy of auspicious rites (*maṅgala*) toward the destruction of obstacles is sublated by positive deviation (*anvaya-vyabhicāra*)—since such rites are performed by persons who are already free from obstacles—and that consequently the Veda lacks authority because it conveys a sublated meaning; [Response: This is not so. For, just as the cognition of fire produced by the word "fire" is not sublated even when no fire is perceived due to the distance or other conditions obstructing its perception, so too the cognition of the destruction of obstacles produced by the word "auspicious rite" is not sublated even when no destruction of obstacles is perceived, due to the distance or other conditions obstructing its perception. Therefore, there is no lack of authority for the Veda on this account. Furthermore, since the destruction of obstacles is a future event, it is not perceived at the time of the performance of the rite; thus, the absence of perception does not constitute a sublation of the Vedic statement. Moreover, the fact that the destruction of obstacles is a future event is established by the very nature of the action, which is a means to a desired end. Consequently, there is no contradiction with the Veda. Thus, the Veda is authoritative. This concludes the section on the authority of the Veda. Now begins the section on the authoritativeness of Smṛti. [The opponent asks: Is the Smṛti authoritative or not? [The proponent replies: It is authoritative. Why? Because it is composed by those who are trustworthy (*āpta*). Who are these trustworthy persons? They are those who possess direct knowledge of Dharma and who have compassion for others. Since they are omniscient, they are trustworthy persons. And since the Smṛti is composed by them, it is authoritative. [The opponent asks: How is it known that they are omniscient? [The proponent replies: It is known through inference. Just as the existence of fire is inferred from smoke, so too the existence of omniscience is inferred from the composition of the Smṛti. [The opponent asks: What is the inferential mark (*liṅga*) here? [The proponent replies: The composition of the Smṛti is the inferential mark. [The opponent asks: What is the pervasion (*vyāpti*) here? [The proponent replies: Whosoever composes a work that is consistent with the truth and free from defects is omniscient, just as the Buddha is. And the Smṛti is a work consistent with the truth and free from defects. Therefore, it is established that the Smṛti is authoritative. This concludes the section on the authoritativeness of Smṛti. Now begins the section on the non-authoritativeness of the Purāṇas. [The opponent asks: Are the Purāṇas authoritative or not? [The proponent replies: They are not authoritative. Why? Because they contain contradictions. For example, some Purāṇas state that the world is eternal, while others state that it is non-eternal. Since there is a contradiction between them, they cannot both be authoritative. Furthermore, they contain many statements that are inconsistent with the Veda. Therefore, the Purāṇas are not authoritative. This concludes the section on the non-authoritativeness of the Purāṇas. Now begins the section on the authoritativeness of the Āgamas. [The opponent asks: Are the Āgamas authoritative or not? [The proponent replies: They are authoritative. Why? Because they are composed by those who are trustworthy. Who are these trustworthy persons? They are the Siddhas and the Yogins who possess direct knowledge of Dharma. Since they are omniscient, they are trustworthy persons. And since the Āgamas are composed by them, they are authoritative. [The opponent asks: How is it known that they are omniscient? [The proponent replies: It is known through inference. Just as the existence of fire is inferred from smoke, so too the existence of omniscience is inferred from the composition of the Āgamas. [The opponent asks: What is the inferential mark here? [The proponent replies: The composition of the Āgamas is the inferential mark. [The opponent asks: What is the pervasion here? [The proponent replies: Whosoever composes a work that is consistent with the truth and free from defects is omniscient, just as the Buddha is. And the Āgamas are works consistent with the truth and free from defects. Therefore, it is established that the Āgamas are authoritative. This concludes the section on the authoritativeness of the Āgamas. Now begins the section on the non-authoritativeness of the Lokāyata. [The opponent asks: Is the Lokāyata authoritative or not? [The proponent replies: It is not authoritative. Why? Because it is composed by one who is untrustworthy. Who is this untrustworthy person? He is Cārvāka, who denies the existence of the afterlife and the fruits of actions. Since he is not omniscient, he is an untrustworthy person. And since the Lokāyata was composed by him, it is not authoritative. [The opponent asks: How is it known that he is not omniscient? [The proponent replies: It is known through inference. Just as the non-existence of fire is inferred from the absence of smoke, so too the non-existence of omniscience is inferred from the denial of the afterlife and the fruits of actions. [The opponent asks: What is the inferential mark here? [The proponent replies: The denial of the afterlife and the fruits of actions is the inferential mark. [The opponent asks: What is the pervasion here? [The proponent replies: Whosoever denies the afterlife and the fruits of actions is not omniscient, just as Cārvāka is. And Cārvāka denies the afterlife and the fruits of actions. Therefore, it is established that the Lokāyata is not authoritative. This concludes the section on the non-authoritativeness of the Lokāyata. Now begins the section on the authoritativeness of the Arthaśāstra. [The opponent asks: Is the Arthaśāstra authoritative or not? [The proponent replies: It is authoritative. Why? Because it is composed by Kautilya, who is a trustworthy person regarding matters of worldly policy. Since he possesses expertise in the science of polity, he is a trustworthy person. And since the Arthaśāstra was composed by him, it is authoritative. [The opponent asks: How is it known that he is a trustworthy person regarding worldly policy? [The proponent replies: It is known through his success in policy. Just as a physician is known to be skilled by his patient's recovery, so too Kautilya is known to be a trustworthy person regarding policy by the prosperity of the Maurya dynasty. Therefore, it is established that the Arthaśāstra is authoritative. This concludes the section on the authoritativeness of the Arthaśāstra. Now begins the section on the non-authoritativeness of the Kāmaśāstra. [The opponent asks: Is the Kāmaśāstra authoritative or not? [The proponent replies: It is not authoritative. Why? Because it promotes only sensual pleasure and does not lead to the highest good (*niḥśreyasa*). Since it is contrary to Dharma, it is not authoritative. This concludes the section on the non-authoritativeness of the Kāmaśāstra. Now begins the section on the authoritativeness of the Dharmaśāstras. [The opponent asks: Are the Dharmaśāstras authoritative or not? [The proponent replies: They are authoritative. Why? Because they are composed by Manu and others, who are trustworthy persons. Who are these trustworthy persons? They are those who have directly perceived the Veda and its meaning. Since they are free from passion and delusion, they are trustworthy persons. And since the Dharmaśāstras were composed by them, they are authoritative. [The opponent asks: How is it known that they are trustworthy persons? [The proponent replies: It is known through their consistency with the Veda. Just as a river flowing from a mountain is known to be pure, so too the Dharmaśāstras, being consistent with the Veda, are known to be authoritative. Therefore, it is established that the Dharmaśāstras are authoritative. This concludes the section on the authoritativeness of the Dharmaśāstras. Now begins the section on the relative strength of conflicting authorities. [The opponent asks: When there is a conflict between the Veda, the Smṛti, and the custom (*ācāra*), which is the stronger authority? [The proponent replies: The Veda is the strongest authority. Why? Because it is the source of all. Just as the sun is the source of light, so too the Veda is the source of Dharma. Therefore, when there is a conflict, the Veda prevails. [The opponent asks: But what about the Smṛti? [The proponent replies: The Smṛti is weaker than the Veda, but stronger than custom. Why? Because it is based on the Veda. Just as a reflection is based on an object, so too the Smṛti is based on the Veda. Therefore

In the view of one who accepts that scripture (*śruti*) indicates [the efficacy of] auspicious rites as a cause, he dispels the doubt with the words "And not... (*na ca*). "Of that" refers to the auspicious rite performed by a person free from obstacles.
"Indicating that" refers to [the relationship between] the auspicious rite and the destruction of obstacles.
The meaning is "that which makes known the relation of cause and effect. Regarding the phrase "when there is an obstacle":

thus, in the case shown, since the effect in the form of the destruction of obstacles does not arise due to the absence of its cause in the form of the counter-positive (the obstacle), the causal capacity remains uncontradicted; therefore...

The sense is that the Veda which teaches [the world] to have a cause [of creation] lacks authority. For this very reason, because the counter-positive (the object destroyed) is the cause of destruction, the Veda teaching that [destruction occurs through other means] lacks authority;
the meaning is that the Veda teaching that expiation (*prāyaścitta*) destroys sin lacks authority. [End of Dinakarī. Now, regarding auspiciousness (*maṅgala*):

The recitation of the Vināyaka hymn and the like is not the cause for the destruction of obstacles, because there is an instance of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of the destruction of obstacles produced by such recitation;

for although the Vināyaka hymn itself may be auspicious (*maṅgala*), the recitation—which consists of the striking of the throat in a manner conducive to that [recitation]—is not itself auspicious. Nor is it the case that the Vināyaka hymn [is the cause] through the relation of being the agent of recitation...

It should not be argued that this [recitation] is the destroyer of obstacles and is itself auspicious, and thus there is no deviation [from the rule], because the reading of those very words— such as "all obstacles are pacified"—
also makes known its quality of being a destroyer of obstacles. [This applies] to the destruction of obstacles produced by expiatory rites (*prāyaścitta*).

Because there is deviation [from this rule], he says: "And auspiciousness (*maṅgala*) also. By the phrase "due to the recitation of hymns," etc., the inclusion of expiatory rites (*prāyaścitta*) is intended. Thus, auspiciousness [functions] through the relation of co-occurrence in the same locus (*svasāmānādhikaraṇya*) and the relation of being produced in the moment immediately following it (*svāvyavahitottarakṣaṇotpattikatva*).

The delimitor of the effect (*kāryatāvacchedaka*) is either the state of being the destruction of obstacles distinguished by auspiciousness (*maṅgala*), or the state of being the destruction of obstacles of a different class (*vijātīya*). Similarly, through the relationship shown, the reading of the Vināyaka hymn and so forth has as its effect-delimiter the state of being the destruction of obstacles distinguished by the reading of the Vināyaka hymn, or the state of being the destruction of obstacles of a different class.

The sense is that there is no deviation [in the inference], because [the absence of obstacles] is the delimitor of the effect (*kāryatāvacchedaka*). Now, if the destruction of obstacles alone were the fruit of the auspicious rite (*maṅgala*), then one who desires completion would not engage in the auspicious rite; therefore, [it is held that] because it is the means for the destruction of obstacles, which is itself the means for completion, [one engages in the rite].

The motivation for [the performance of the rite] must be stated; however, that is not possible, because in cases where the absence of obstacles is self-evident, there is a deviation (vyabhicāra), since the destruction of obstacles cannot be the means for completion [of the work].

He dispels this doubt with the words "In some cases... [and so on]. But if this is so, there is a lack of uniformity (ananugama); therefore, [he provides the definition] by way of a uniform characteristic (*anugata-rūpa*).

He states the seed (the underlying reason) for its being a cause: "pratibandhaka... [meaning] "of the absence of connection, by way of being an absence of connection. Thus, the sense is that because it is a cause by way of being the absence of connection with obstacles (*vighna*), there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) from what was stated previously. And here, [it is] by way of the absence of each respective obstacle...
It should be understood that [the cause] is the causal state itself, and not the collection of absences of obstacles;

for since the prior non-existence of obstacles and so forth cannot coexist in one place, the completion [of the work] would otherwise be impossible. Furthermore, in cases where completion occurs even without an auspicious rite (*maṅgala*), [the cause] exists in that which lacks the destruction of obstacles.

Having raised the suspicion of a deviation from the negative concomitance (*vyatireka-vyabhicāra*) because completion [of a work] is observed even in the absence of such [auspicious acts], he refutes it with the words "And thus" (*itthaṃ ca*). He says "established by itself" (*svataḥ-siddha*) because of the excessive complexity (*gaurava*) involved in postulating the destruction of evil (*durita-dhvaṃsa*) and, consequently, postulating the auspicious rite (*maṅgala*) as its cause. And where, even though the auspicious rite is present, [the desired result does not occur]... *The Dinakarī:* And where, even though the auspicious rite is present, [the desired result does not occur]...

It should be understood that completion occurs there because of auspiciousness (*maṅgala*), and the destruction of obstacles (*vighna*) certainly follows; however, the absence of completion may result either from an abundance of obstacles or from an obstacle arising immediately after the auspicious rite.
Now, how can there be a causal relationship between completion and the destruction of obstacles, both of which reside in the self (*ātman*), which is as pervasive as space?

To this it is replied: by the relation of being the motivator of its own counter-positive, the absence of the connection with obstacles—characterized as the non-existence of the connection with obstacles—is the cause of completion, which consists in the destruction of the final phoneme, by way of the relation of qualification (*viśeṣaṇatā*). In reality, however, by the word "they say" (*āhuḥ*),...

He clarifies the "otherwise established" nature (anyathāsiddhi) indicated [by the previous argument] with the words "in some cases": by the restrictive particle *eva* in the phrase "only the absolute absence of obstacles," there is an exclusion of both the destruction of obstacles and the auspicious rite (maṅgala) that serves as its means. It is the cause of completion (*samāpti-sādhana*), because it exists immediately prior to the completion.

This is certain. And thus, since the completion [of the work] at the auspicious site is already established by that very fact, both the auspicious rite (*maṅgala*) and the destruction of obstacles produced by it are rendered superfluous (*anyathāsiddhi*).
For there is no evidence for a contradiction between destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) and prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) on the grounds of their absolute absence (*atyantābhāva*).
The meaning is that in the case of destruction (*dhvaṃsa*), there is an absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) [of the obstructer].
Now, one might object: "Let the causal efficacy (*hetutā*) belong simply to being an absence other than mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva-bhinna-abhāvatva*), as this is simpler.
To this, he says: "In the presence of an obstructer... [and so on]. Even when an obstructer is present... [end of Dinakarī].

Since there exists an absence delimited by another relation [such as conjunction], in order to prevent the production of the effect, causality must be stated precisely as an absence whose counter-correlativity is delimited by that specific relation; therefore,
destruction (dhvaṃsa) cannot be the cause, because it is not delimited by such a relation.
The sense is that there is a lack of proof. The destruction of evil (duritadhvaṃsa) is brought about by the causal complex for the destruction of evil;

it is self-established as being brought about by the absence of the causes of evil. By this, [it is shown that] the investigation into whether the destruction of obstacles or their absolute non-existence is the cause of completion is irrelevant to the present subject matter.

In establishing that [as the cause], it is of no use for the subject at hand. Thus, if the collection (*kūṭa*) of absences of obstructors were the cause, then—since past and future antecedent absences (*prāgabhāva*) and destructions (*dhvaṃsa*) cannot coexist simultaneously—the collection would be unestablished at any one time. This is because, according to the previously mentioned method, the property of having a counter-positive delimited by a particular relation [is required].

The objections—that the destruction (dhvaṃsa) and prior non-existence (prāgabhāva) are not included because they are qualifiers of the absence of an obstructor—are refuted, since, according to the stated method, only the absolute non-existence of an obstructor is the cause for every effect. In the root text, regarding the phrase "nūtana" and so forth: that which is new...
To him whose splendor is like the splendor of a cloud—that is, a rain-cloud;

by this it is indicated that just as a fresh rain-cloud quickly bestows rain, so too does he bestow the fruits desired by his devotees. [This describes] the satisfaction of the Blessed One, who is worthy of salutation.

To indicate this, he says: "He hides at the root" (*mūle gopeti*). The meaning is: for the sake of stealing the *dukūla* garments—the clothes—of those who are the young wives (*vadhūṭī*), the youthful women of the cowherds (*gopa*). Regarding the word "to him" (*tasmai*): the pronoun *tat* is used here to suggest that he is universally renowned among all people. By this...

Having raised the objection that it is improper to state that the Blessed One is the ultimate limit of the removal [of defects] which constitutes the mode of salutation, because there is a lack of proof for the Blessed One's existence,
he says "saṃsāra... to indicate the inference that establishes the Lord according to the Nyāya school.

In order to dispel the misconception that "the tree of saṃsāra" (*saṃsārasya mahīruhaḥ*) is a genitive tatpuruṣa compound, [the author] states in the *Muktāvalī* that it is a karmadhāraya: "saṃsāra eva" (it is saṃsāra itself). Since being a seed (*bījatva*) implies being an inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇatva*), and that is contradicted in the case of God (*Īśvara*), he says: "efficient cause" (*nimitta*). [Objection: But in the case of God...
An auspicious invocation in the form of a salutation is inappropriate because there is no proof for the existence of Īśvara;
for in that regard, perception is not a valid means of knowledge, since [Īśvara], being an incorporeal substance, is not an object of external perception;
nor is mental perception [a proof], because the perception of one's own self by the mind of another is precluded in order to establish the perception of the self.

Since it is necessary that the cause [of cognition] be the contact between the mind and a self that is of a different class and distinct from other selves, such a cause is absent in God. Nor is there inference, due to the absence of a logical mark (liṅga).
Nor is scripture itself, such as "producing heaven and earth," a valid means of proof.
Since the authority of the Vedas (*śruti*) depends upon their being uttered by God, when there is doubt regarding God, the authority of the Vedas is also subject to doubt;
therefore, he says: "By this [it is established]. The means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is of the nature of inference (*anumāna*). Likewise, the earth, sprouts, and so forth [are also established].

Now, what is the delimiting condition (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*) here? It cannot be "earth-ness" (*kṣititva*), for since even sprouts and the like possess earth-ness, it would be redundant to mention them separately. Furthermore, if the intended goal were the establishment of the probandum (*sādhya*) as co-extensive with earth-ness, then in the case of the example, such as a jar, [the probandum would already be established].

In part, there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*). If [the probandum] were to apply by way of the delimiting condition (*avacchedaka*), there would be a contradiction regarding the atom (*paramāṇu*). If "being an earth-entity produced by effort" (*janyakṣititva*) is the delimiting condition of the subject (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*), then according to the opponent's view, the exclusion of the term "produced" (*janyapada-vyāvṛtti*) is unestablished, because in that system there is no earth-entity that is not produced; for [in their view], it is simply "producibility" (*janyatva*) [that is the delimiting condition].

Furthermore, because earthness (*kṣititva*) would be redundant in the scope of the delimiting condition of the subject (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*) due to the possibility of its being *tathātva* (the property to be proven), and because that [earthness] is not even possible—

since it would entail the identity of the delimiting condition of the subject and the reason— if this is argued, we say no; for it is precisely "effectness" (*kāryatva*), in the form of a specific essential relation (*svarūpasaṃbandha*), that serves as the delimiting condition of the subject.

Because the probans is precisely "being an effect," which consists in being the counter-positive of antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*), there is no identity between the two [the probans and the probandum]. Furthermore, the probandum is not "being produced by an immediate cognition, desire to act, and volition directed toward its own material cause," because volition alone is established through positive and negative concomitance as the cause of every effect.
Because the desire to know and the desire to act that produce that [effect] are otherwise established (*anyathāsiddha*) in that case,

there is a sublation (*bādha*) of the probandum (*sādhya*)— defined as being produced by those three— in that instance; furthermore, because there is no single property of "selfhood" (*svatva*) common to both the example and the subject (*pakṣa*),
the probandum defined by that [property], namely "having for its object its own material cause," and so forth, is impossible.
Furthermore, because the status of being an effort whose object is the material cause (*upādāna*) is more complex than the mere status of being an effort,

it cannot serve as the delimiting condition (*avacchedaka*) for causality. Rather, [the effect] resides in the state of being an effect delimited by the relation of inherence (*samavāya*), which is itself defined by a causality delimited by the status of being an effort delimited by the relation of qualificand-ness (*viśeṣyatā*).
Therefore, even though the state of being produced by an effort belonging to us exists in the subject (*pakṣa*) through the medium of *adṛṣṭa* (unseen merit/demerit),

there is no *siddhasādhana* (proving what is already established). And if, in the case of every effect in general, there were positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) solely by way of "effort-ness" (*kṛtitva*), [then this would be the case].

If causality is accepted by way of being a cognition (*jñāna*) or a desire (*icchā*), then let the probandum (*sādhya*) be "being produced by such a cognition," "being produced by a desire," or "being produced by an effort" (*kṛti*). As for the claim that the probandum is simply "being produced by an agent" (*kartṛjanya*), that is not correct;

for there is no evidence that agency (*kartṛtva*) is the cause in respect to every effect, and because of parsimony (*lāghava*), it is simply by way of being an effort (*kṛtitva*) that [effort] is the cause therein.

Because it is a cause. Now, does it not follow that the following inference is established: "The effect possesses a producedness delimited by the relation of inherence, which is defined by a generative capacity residing in the action and delimited by the relation of qualificandness, because it is the counter-positive of a prior non-existence"? And in that case, [the argument applies] to destruction (*dhvaṃsa*), which is included within the scope of "producedness" as the delimiting factor of the subjecthood (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*). *Note: The text fragment provided ends abruptly with "ie2> dinakarī| pakṣatāvacchedakajanyatvākrānte". The term "dinakarī" refers to the commentary on the *Nyāyasiddhāntamuktāvalī* by Mahādeva Bhaṭṭa, known as the *Dinakarī*. The phrase "pakṣatāvacchedakajanyatvākrānte" means "that which is encompassed by the 'producedness' which serves as the delimiting factor of the subjecthood."*

If it is argued that there is a contradiction (*bādha*) because of the absence of the probandum— defined as being produced by means of the relation of inherence (*samavāya*), which is in turn defined by the generative power residing in the action (*kṛti*) as delimited by the relation of qualificandness (*viśeṣyatā*)— we say no;
for [the probandum] is simply "being produced" as qualified by existence (*sattva*), which excludes destruction (*dhvaṃsa*).

Because [the property] is accepted as the delimiting condition of the subject (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*). Nor should it be argued that there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) due to the absence of the aforementioned probandum (*sādhya*) in the destruction (*dhvaṃsa*), which is the locus of the reason (*hetu*); for the reason is qualified by the adjunct of existence (*sattva-vaiśiṣṭya*). Even if deviation is thus excluded by this method, if destruction were produced by volitional effort (*kṛti-janyatva*)...
If it is argued that the common doctrine—that every effect is produced by volitional effort (*kṛti*)—would be contradicted by the absence of such effort [in the case of destruction], we say no;

for such a doctrine is unworthy of credence because it lacks logical justification. Alternatively, let "merely being produced" (*janyatvamātra*), which is common to both [produced things] and destruction (*dhvaṃsa*), be the delimiting factor of the subject (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*), and let "merely being produced by volitional effort" (*kṛtijanyatvamātra*) be the probandum (*sādhya*).

And thus, even regarding the reason (*hetu*), the qualification "by a sentient being" (*sattva-vaiśiṣṭya*) need not be adopted, as there is no purpose for it. Likewise, since the property of being produced by the volition of God (*īśvara-yatna-janyatva*) is unassailable even in the case of destruction (*dhvaṃsa*), the doctrine that "everything that is an effect is produced by volition" (*kāryamātre kṛti-janyatva-pravāda*) is also justified. Nor does it follow that if mere "being produced by volition" were the probandum (*sādhya*), [the argument would fail] through the medium of the unseen merit/demerit (*adṛṣṭa*).

It should not be argued that there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) by taking as the object [of the probandum] the fact of being produced by an effort of ours directed toward the sacrificial offering (*havis*) and so forth;

for the property of "being produced by an effort" must be qualified by the condition "not mediated by the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*). This is the general direction [of the argument]. In such an inference, through the assistance of the cognition of parsimony (*lāghava*), [the conclusion is reached]. (Dinakarī)

Since eternity and oneness appear in respect to [God's] knowledge, will, and action, the establishment of His eternal oneness follows. Now, what kind of oneness is the object apprehended by inference regarding God’s knowledge and so forth? It cannot be oneness in the form of a number, because qualities are not admitted to reside in qualities. Nor...

It must be stated that the object of that [inference] is oneness, which consists in the state of not being a delimitor of the counter-correlativity of a difference residing in that which possesses eternal cognition;
for such oneness is not present prior to the inference of eternal cognition, and thus [cannot be the object] in such an inference.

If it is argued that this is impossible, some here [reply]: through the relation of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), the unity residing in the substratum appears in the inferential cognition regarding knowledge and so forth; or rather, the object of that [cognition] is unity in the form of not being coreferential with duality. And there is no coreferentiality with the duality residing in both the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*) in the Lord’s knowledge and so forth.

It should not be said that there is a contradiction because [the property] exists in six [substances]; for duality must be qualified by the condition of not subsisting in suffering (duḥkha) and so forth.
Nor should it be said that even so there is a contradiction because the co-existence (sāmānādhikaraṇya) of duality residing in a jar and God exists therein;
for [duality] must also be qualified by the condition of not subsisting in either self (ātman) or non-self (anātman).

They say that this is because duality must be qualified [by unity]. That is not correct; for even if one accepts two cognitions in God, the intended object is not established by the mere possibility of such a presentation of unity.
In reality, however...
Unity is simply the state of having a cognition that is not distinct from its own substratum.

This should be understood in the same way regarding the will (*icchā*) and action (*kṛti*) of the Lord (*īśvara*). And thus, when such cognition and the rest are established, [the quality of] being a quality (*guṇatva*) resides therein.
In the *Dinakarī*:

When it is to be proved by means of a reason (*hetu*) that [the subject] is dependent on a substance (*dravyāśritatva*), the establishment of God (*Īśvara*) follows because there is a sublation (*bādha*) regarding any other substance; this is how it should be understood. "Because of being non-conclusive" (*aprayojakatvāt*): the sense is that there is an absence of a favorable argument (*anukūlatarka*).

This is an illustration. In the case of the reason "not being produced by a body," even though the qualification "body" serves to exclude the unestablished (asiddhi), it is redundant because it does not exclude deviation (vyabhicāra). Consequently, since it is possible to grasp the pervasion (vyāpti) as delimited by that qualification [only when the deviation is excluded], [the qualification is unnecessary].
It should also be observed that "unestablished due to lack of pervasion" (*vyāpyatvāsiddhi*) is likewise applicable.

Nor should it be argued that although the presence of a redundant qualification (*vyarthaviśeṣaṇatva*) constitutes a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) for the opponent, there is no evidence that the cognition of such a qualification acts as an obstacle to the cognition of pervasion (*vyāpti*); for even so, [it does].

Because the property of the Guru (the probans) lacks a delimiting factor (*anavacchedakatā*), the pervasion (*vyāpti*)—defined as possessing a property that delimits the relation to the probandum (*sādhyasambandhitāvacchedakadharmavattva*)—is absent therein;
thus, the fallacy of unestablished pervasion (*vyāpyatvāsiddhi*) is unavoidable. As it was stated by the Teacher: "For one who attempts to avoid one kind of non-establishment..."

Regarding the phrase "the second [is] the substratum": it is precisely the causal relation between agent and effect, defined by agency and being an effect. Nor is there an absence of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) for that which is delimited by potness (*ghaṭatva*) and so forth.
It should not be argued that there is no evidence for such a causal relation because the potter and others function as causes toward a jar solely by virtue of being agents (kartṛtva).

Rather than postulating an infinite number of cause-and-effect relations based on distinctions such as "pot-ness" and "cloth-ness," it is more appropriate to postulate a single causal relation where "being produced" (*kāryatva*) is the effect and "effort" (*kṛti*) is the cause; this is in accordance with the maxim: "Whatever applies to two particulars [applies to their general classes]."
Furthermore, because of the necessity of a general relation between effect and agent based on the properties of being an effect (*kāryatva*) and being produced (*kṛtatva*),

one cannot argue that such a principle is without proof; for it would involve unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*) to postulate that the entire collection of absences of specific agents (*tattatkṛti-abhāva-kūṭa*) is the cause of the absence of things subsumed under the property of being an effect (*kāryatva-avacchinna-abhāva*).

This is because there is parsimony (*lāghava*) in positing a single absence delimited by "being an effect" (*kṛtitvāvacchinnābhāva*) as the causal condition (*prayojaka*). However, some [hold that] even if "being an effect" is not the delimitor of the effect-ness of effort (*kṛti*), nevertheless, since effort is a cause with respect to things delimited by "jar-ness" (*ghaṭatva*) and so on, one may take a jar existing at the time of the beginning of creation as the subject (*pakṣa*) and prove [the existence of God] by means of the reason "jar-ness" and so forth.

They say that the existence of God is established because the [existence of] living beings is sublated when proving that [the world] has an agent. The authors of the *Dīdhiti*, however, maintain that even if volition (*kṛti*) is not the cause for that which is delimited by "being an effect" (*kāryatva*),
it is nonetheless the cause for that which is delimited by "being a jar" (*ghaṭatva*) and so forth, because of the production of a broken jar.
They state that the existence of God is established as the substratum of that [action], because action necessarily presupposes a prior agent.

Now, one might object: in this manner, based on positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) between the pot and so forth and the activity of the potter and so forth, activity (as a general property) is the cause for that which is delimited by "being an effect" (*kāryatva*); consequently, since sprouts and the like arise...
If it is argued that a permanent body for God might be established on the basis of His prior volitional effort (*pūrva-ceṣṭā*), we say no;

for by such positive and negative concomitances (*anvaya-vyatireka*), action (*kriyā*) as a class is the cause with respect to that which is delimited by being an effect (*kāryatva-avacchinna*), and there is no evidence for action-as-effort (*ceṣṭātva*) to be the cause in that context. However, those who follow the opinion of the Teacher (Vallabha) maintain: let it be so.

Since effort (*ceṣṭā*) is the cause in that case, let there be for God an eternal body in accordance with that [requirement]; nevertheless, this does not establish a body distinct from [the atoms], because it is accepted that the atoms themselves constitute His body.
And thus, [the world is produced] by means of bodies in the form of atoms which possess effort generated by the creative act of God.

The production of various effects occurs; and since a specific dissimilarity (*vaijātya*) consisting of the nature of effort (*ceṣṭātva*) is admitted in the activity of atoms, and because the definition of a body does not include the property of being a final composite (*antyāvayavitva*), there is no impossibility of atoms being bodies. Nor [is there a problem] regarding multiple atoms...
It should not be argued that its status as a distinct entity is established by parsimony (lāghava) due to the complexity (gaurava) involved in conceiving it as the skin of the body;

for if that [self] were large (mahat), it would be impossible for it to enter into stones and the like without bending, which would result in the logical impossibility of producing the body of a frog within a stone. Furthermore, if it were minute (aṇu), it would be impossible for it to produce effects located at a distance. Thus they say; enough of this.

Regarding the phrase "by means of sprouts": as for the claim that in the previously mentioned proof by *sthāpanā* (establishment), "being produced by a body" (*śarīrajanyatva*) is a *upādhi* (limiting condition)— because it pervades the probandum (*sādhya*) in the case of a jar and the like,
yet does not pervade the probans (*sādhana*) in the case of a sprout and the like— and because [the opponent argues] that in the case of a sprout...

It should not be argued that because there is doubt regarding the probandum in the form of having an agent, there is doubt as to whether the condition (upādhi) pervades the probandum, and thus no certainty regarding its being a condition can be established; for even so, the status of being a doubtful condition remains unavoidable. Nor does the [fallacy] introduced by doubt regarding the condition...

It should not be argued that doubt regarding deviation—specifically, doubt regarding deviation in the subject (pakṣa) itself—is not an obstacle [to inference]; for even doubt regarding deviation in both the subject and its similar instances (sapakṣa) acts as an obstacle.

It is for this very reason that, in the absence of favorable reasoning (anukūlatarka), "being other than the subject" (pakṣetaratva) is designated as a suspected extraneous condition (sandigdhopādhi).
The author of the commentary [says] "it is consistent"; that is not so, because [the relation is] by way of being an effect and being an effort (kṛti).

Because, through the existence of a favorable *tarka* consisting of the relation of cause and effect, there is a certainty that the reason (*hetu*)—namely, "being an effect"—is pervaded by the probandum (*sādhya*);

and because, since the *upādhi* does not pervade what is pervaded by the probandum, there is a certainty that the *upādhi* does not pervade the probandum. And thus, when God is established by the aforementioned inference...
He states that the Veda is also a means of valid cognition regarding God because its authority is ascertained through the fact that it was uttered by Him:

"Generating heaven and earth," and so forth. By the phrase "and so forth," he includes such passages as: "One should meditate upon God," "He who is all-knowing is all-perceiving," and "Whose austerity consists of knowledge."

This includes [the scriptural passages] such as "He desired" (*sokāmayata*). Furthermore, inference from the effect is illustrative; for instance, the motion that causes the formation of a binary atomic compound at the time of creation must be produced by volition, because it is a motion. Also, the absence of falling in things possessing gravity [is due to an unseen force].
The maintenance [of the world] is caused by an effort that prevents falling, because it is a form of maintenance, like the absence of flight in a bird;
the destruction of the cosmic egg is produced by an effort, because it is a destruction, like the destruction of a water-pot;
and the conventional usage regarding pots and such is prompted by an independent person, because it is a conventional usage, like modern invented scripts and the like.

The valid cognition produced by the Veda is generated by the speaker’s knowledge of the true meaning of the sentence, because it is a verbal valid cognition, like the valid cognition produced by Caitra’s sentence; the Veda was composed by a person who is not subject to saṃsāra, because it is the Veda;
the Veda is of human origin, because it consists of sentences; and whatever is not so [composed by a non-saṃsāric person] is not so [the Veda].
"Just as poetry" is a negative example (*vyatirekadṛṣṭānta*), like the *Mahābhārata*.

There are also other inferences, either direct or indirect, such as: "The number that produces the dimension (*parimāṇa*) of a binary atomic compound (*dvyaṇuka*) is produced by a relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*), because it is a number other than oneness. Dinakari. iе2>.
The proofs for the existence of God (Īśvara) are [to be understood] through awakening.
As it has been said: "From the effect, from design, from maintenance, and so forth;
from the word, from cognition, from sneezing, from the sentence, and from a specific number—the immutable Lord is to be proven. (Verse 1) Design (*āyojana*)...

Action (*karman*) is that by which one goes; it is a "path" (*pada*), meaning worldly discourse—this is the summary. At the beginning of the root text, he makes a formal declaration for the student's attention: "Substance, quality... (and so on). The words "are defined" are to be supplied as the ellipsis. [The author holds that] action is not distinct from conjunction (*saṃyoga*).

The word "likewise" (*tathā*) was stated in order to refute the view of the author of the *Bhūṣaṇa*; the meaning is that just as quality (*guṇa*) is a distinct category of reality (*padārtha*), so too is action (*karman*). Furthermore, the word "likewise" was stated again to refute the Prābhākara position that non-existence (*abhāva*) is merely of the nature of its locus (*adhikaraṇātman*); the reasoning for this will be explained later.

Although the number seven is obtained from the enumerative sentence itself by virtue of its exclusion of numbers both less than and greater than seven, nevertheless, the explicit mention of "seven" is for the sake of clarity. [An objection: But why are other categories (padārthas) not mentioned? To this he says: "They have been proclaimed. Likewise...
The meaning is that there are no categories other than these, because they have not been mentioned by Kaṇāda and others. (Dinakari)
Now, one might raise the objection: "In other treatises, six categories of existence (bhāva-padārtha) and a seventh, non-existence (abhāva), have been described;

why has it not been described in the same way here? Anticipating this, he says: "In the Muktāvalī, of the seventh... Here, [the meaning is] that there is a state of being existent through the relation of inherence (samavāya) or through another relation such as inherence in the same object (ekārthasamavāya).

"Being-ness" (bhāvatva) [is the definition of existence], and the absence of that is "non-being-ness" (abhāvatva). "Obtained" means obtained by implication. "By that state of being obtained. "Separate presentation" means presentation as being-ness; the word "of them" is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence]. Now, one might object: why are other categories not mentioned, since the *Nyāyasūtra* defines only sixteen categories? Anticipating this doubt:

Even in the view of the Naiyāyikas, it is not contradictory that there are seven categories (*padārtha*), because the sixteen categories are included within these seven; thus he says: "And these... He provides the support of the Bhāṣya for the stated point: "And it has been established... [He adds]: "In this very way."

The meaning is that it has been established that there are exactly seven categories—substance, quality, action, generality, particularity, inherence, and absence—because the sixteen [categories] of the Nyāya school are included within these very ones.
If one asks how they are included, it is as follows: the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), such as the sense organs, are included within substance (*dravya*).
In the absence of defects, there is pervasion regarding the following: with respect to the substance that is the object of knowledge—consisting of the self, the body, and the sense organs;

with respect to the quality that is the object—consisting of smell, taste, form, touch, and sound; with respect to the quality that is cognition; with respect to the substance that is the mind; with respect to the quality that is activity; and with respect to the defects consisting of desire, aversion, and false knowledge.

Regarding the qualities of those who are led away from the states of passion, hatred, and delusion: the term *pretyabhāva* (rebirth) has as its basis for application (*pravṛttinimitta*) the state of being born after dying; according to the etymology "existence after having died," it is the state of birth following death.
Death is the destruction of the final conjunction between the vital breaths and the body, while birth is the initial conjunction between the body and the vital breaths.
Likewise, immediately after its destruction, that [action] which consists of such a conjunction is included within the quality (guṇa);

the primary fruit, which consists of the experience of pleasure or pain, is included within the quality; and even the fruit consisting of the mere produced state common to both primary and secondary results is included within substance (dravya) and so forth; and suffering, characterized by affliction, is included within the quality.

Apavarga, however, is the absolute cessation of suffering. Sufferings are twenty-one in number: the body, the six sense organs, the six objects, the six types of cognition, pleasure, and pain. Among these, [the cessation applies] to the body and so forth, which are devoid of the universal property of "suffering-ness" (duḥkhatva).
The state of being suffering (*duḥkhatva*) is secondary (*gauṇa*) by virtue of its connection with suffering;
that is, even pleasure such as that of heaven is unimpededly connected to suffering through the cognition of its destruction.
Nor [can it be argued] that because the mind and the ear—two among the twenty-one types of suffering—are eternal, how [could they be suffering]?

It should be stated that it is the destruction of that [organ]. For when the specific form of the auditory organ (*śravaṇa*), which constitutes suffering by being a cause of pain through the mediation of cognition, is destroyed by the destruction of the ear-cavity (*karṇaśaṣkulī*), there follows the destruction of the suffering consisting of the auditory organ characterized by that form.

Thus, it is precisely the mind, when engaged in activity in the form of conjunction with the self, that constitutes suffering by being the cause of suffering through the medium of cognition; [this holds] because, upon the cessation of that activity,
there is no longer simultaneity with the suffering characterized by that [active] mind.

If it is asked: "In that case, if liberation is the destruction of such suffering, how can it be accomplished by the knowledge of reality (tattvajñāna)?"—the answer is as follows: through the knowledge of reality, the latent impressions (vāsanās) of false knowledge are destroyed;
and when the latent impressions are destroyed, there is an absence of defects such as passion characterized by those impressions.
Because there is an absence of the qualified when the qualifier is absent, and because there is an absence of the cause consisting of such passion and the like,
there is an absence— meaning non-arising— of activity in the form of merit and demerit; and when that does not arise, there is an absence of birth,
which consists of the connection with another body following the exhaustion of the body governed by *prārabdha*-karma.

The cessation of karma—both that which has begun to bear fruit (*prārabdha*) and that which is different from it—occurs through the knowledge of the true nature of enjoyment (*bhoga*). In the absence of birth, there is no arising of suffering; thus, regarding the constituent part of the definition consisting in "not being simultaneous with suffering residing in the same locus":
Since the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) is the instrumental cause of liberation, liberation is to be accomplished through the knowledge of reality;

thus says the Sūtra: "Upon the successive removal of false knowledge, defects, activity, birth, and suffering, there follows the removal of each subsequent one, resulting in liberation. The meaning of this is as follows: among the items enumerated beginning with birth...

In the middle, due to the disappearance of each subsequent [member] of the series, there is the absence of its immediate predecessor, because of the absence of that which is directly prior. And thus, by the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*) is destroyed; by that, the non-arising of activity (*pravṛtti*); and by that, [the destruction] of the defects (*doṣa*).

Destruction [of suffering] results from that [knowledge], and from that destruction comes the non-arising of birth, and from that the non-arising of suffering; thus the previously stated meaning is established. However, they say that the destruction of the twenty-one kinds of suffering is to be accomplished by its own specific causes, and that in that regard, the knowledge of reality (tattvajñāna) is not the instrumental cause.
The Navyas (modern Naiyāyikas), however, maintain that since the destruction of a particular quality in a fit and all-pervading substance is caused by its immediately succeeding quality,
liberation in the form of the destruction of suffering is possible through the very quality produced immediately after it; therefore,
[the aforementioned view] is not [necessary] there.
In the *Dinakarī*,

it is stated that since [nescience] depends upon the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), the word "suffering" (*duḥkha*) should be interpreted as referring to "demerit" (*durita*), which is the means to suffering; and because demerit lacks the nature of being a quality (*guṇa*), it cannot be destroyed by a quality produced subsequently.

They say that liberation, which consists in the destruction of that [suffering], is indeed achievable through the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*). Thus, in the absence of such liberation, [the categories are established as follows]: doubt resides in the category of quality (*guṇa*);
purpose, in the form of an object of desire to be accomplished, resides in substance (*dravya*) and the other categories as appropriate; and so forth.

The example (*dṛṣṭānta*), which is the object of a certainty possessing the probandum, the probans, or both, [is included] among substance (*dravya*) and the other categories as appropriate. The tenet (*siddhānta*), consisting of objects established by various scriptures, is included among substance and the other categories.

The members (*avayava*)—such as the proposition (*pratijñā*) and others, which are of the nature of the form of the word itself—are included among quality (*guṇa*). [This occurs] through the superimposition of the pervader (*vyāpyāropa*).

It serves as a quality for the reductio ad absurdum (tarka) which consists in the attribution of the pervader; it serves as a quality for the ascertainment (nirṇaya); it serves as a quality for discussion (vāda), which is a form of discourse by one desiring to know the truth; it serves as a quality for disputation (jalpa), which is a form of discourse by one desiring victory;
and it serves as a quality for cavil (vitaṇḍā), which is a form of discourse devoid of the establishment of one's own position.

The fallacies of the reason (*hetvābhāsa*)—which consist of the nature of that which is the object of an inference, its cause, or any other obstructing cognition—are each included within the categories of substance (*dravya*) and so forth, as appropriate. As for quibble (*chala*), which consists in the statement of a refutation by imagining a different meaning for a word used with a specific intention: [...]* *Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly; the translation reflects the portion available.*

Regarding the category of quality (*guṇa*): since the genus of "non-existence" (*asattva*) is not a quality, the points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*), which consist in the apprehension of the nature of the cause of defeat, are included, as appropriate,
within substance (*dravya*) and the other categories.
The points of defeat (nigrahasthāna) are: loss of the proposition (pratijñāhāni), shifting the proposition (pratijñāntara), contradiction (pratirodha),

renunciation of the proposition (pratijñāsaṃnyāsa), shifting the reason (hetvantara), irrelevant matter (arthāntara), the meaningless (nirarthaka), the unintelligible (avijñātārthaka), the incoherent (apārthaka), the mistimed (aprāptakāla), the deficient (nyūna), and the redundant (adhika).

Repetition, non-reproduction, ignorance, lack of ingenuity, distraction, admission of the opponent's position, overlooking what is censurable, censuring what is not censurable, deviation from a tenet, and fallacious reasons.
Here, the word "and" (ca) serves to include those not explicitly mentioned; by this, the [fallacy of] the example is included.

The inclusion of deficiencies in the means of proof (*sādhanavaikalya*) and so forth. Regarding this, in the absence of "abandoning the proposition" (*pratijñāhāni*), which consists in the relinquishing of the subject (*pakṣa*) and other elements specifically promised, there is the statement of a matter already understood from another [source], characterized by a qualification not previously stated, with the desire to refute a fault alleged by the opponent. This is the *dinakarī*.
Regarding the merit of a different proposition (*pratijñāntara*):

it refers to the merit of a contradiction with one's own proposition (*pratijñāvirodha*), which consists in stating a reason (*hetu*) and so forth that contradicts the thesis (*sādhya*) and other elements stated by oneself;
[and] when the thesis and other elements stated by oneself have been refuted by an opponent, [it refers to] the form of abandoning that very thesis.

In the absence of an abandonment of the thesis (*pratijñā-saṃnyāsa*), it is a merit to state another reason (*hetvantara*) consisting of a reason qualified by a delimitor of the causal status (*hetutāvacchedaka*) other than the previously stated delimitor of the causal status, with the desire to refute a criticism raised by the opponent; it is a merit to state a different matter (*arthāntara*) consisting of the expression of something not required by the context; and it is a merit to employ words that are non-expressive (*avācaka*), which constitutes the meaningless (*nirarthaka*).

The fault of *avijñātārtha* (meaningless) consists in the employment of a sentence whose meaning is not understood due to the use of non-expressive words; it also consists in the employment of a sentence that fails to produce an understanding for the assembly and the opponent because it does not generate a presentation conducive to such comprehension. The fault of *apārthaka* (incoherent) consists in the employment of words devoid of the expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) necessary for the understanding of the intended sentence-meaning.
Regarding the excellence [of the response]:

it consists in the excellence of that which is "untimely" (*aprāptakāla*), which takes the form of an utterance following a sequence contrary to the order of the discourse that serves as the basis for the established convention;
and it consists in the excellence of that which is "deficient" (*nyūna*), which takes the form of an utterance of a member [of the syllogism] lacking some constituent part.
In the category of *adhika* (redundancy), there is the inclusion of that which consists in the statement of an additional reason (*hetu*) and so forth;

in the category of *punarukta* (repetition), there is the inclusion of that which consists in restating what has already been said; and in the absence of *ananubhāṣaṇa* (failure to restate), which consists in not repeating [the opponent's argument] even though it has been stated three times by the assembly (*pariṣad*). By the assembly...
In the absence of ignorance, which consists in the failure to understand the meaning of what has been stated three times by the proponent;
and in the absence of lack of ingenuity (apratibhā), which consists in the failure to produce a reply despite having understood the opponent's statement;
[and] by pointing out an impossibility, such as an attachment to other duties at another time.

In the absence of distraction, which consists of the cessation of the discourse; in the absence of "conceding the point" (*matānujñā*), which consists of failing to point out a fault in one's own position while pointing out a fault in the opponent's position; and in the absence of "overlooking the censurable" (*paryanuyojyopekṣaṇa*), which consists of failing to point out a ground for defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) when one has reached such a ground.

In the absence of an occasion for a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*), there is the merit of "reproaching one who is not to be reproached" (*niranuyojyānuyoga*), which consists in the statement of such a point of defeat at an improper time. In the absence of "contradiction of tenet" (*apasiddhānta*), which consists in deviating from a tenet accepted during the discussion,
the fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*)— possessing the previously stated definitions— are included within [the categories of] substance (*dravya*) and so forth.
Anticipating the objection that the *Bhāṣya* may be of non-Vedic origin (*anārṣa*), he states the consensus of the authors of the *Maṇi* and other works with the words "iti eva" (thus indeed).

To prevent the production of burning upon the presence of a jewel (*maṇi*) and other such factors, one must assert that the jewel and so forth possess the status of a "non-obstructer" (*apratibandhaka*) consisting in their being "dissociators of the causal complex" (*kāraṇavighaṭaka*). And this...

[The counteracting power] functions precisely as the destroyer of the cause, which consists of a capacity conducive to the burning [of fuel] that culminates in an increase in size; for such a power is established by the fact that the obstructive nature of the *maṇi* jewel and other such objects would otherwise be inexplicable. Since this power is not included among the six categories of existence (*ṣaṭpadārtha*), it is distinct [from them]. Thus says the *Dinakarī*. These are the categories of things.

With the intention that the root text’s statement "seven are proclaimed" is incorrect, the Prābhākara raises an objection with "But surely... (*nanu*). Regarding the term "distinct" (*atirikta*): it means distinct from the seven categories (*padārtha*). He establishes the status of this distinct category by means of the passage beginning with "For instance" (*tathā hi*), and so forth.

By the phrase "maṇyādi" (jewel, etc.), the inclusion of mantras, medicinal herbs, and so forth is intended. "Samavahatena" means being present nearby. Now, one might object: since burning does not occur simply due to the absence of the cause, namely fire, the jewel and other such things cannot be considered obstructors; therefore, it is specified as "by fire being present."

Burning is either the production of another form or the transformation of the previous form. The author refutes the status of anything other than the gem as an obstructer with the words "by its absence" (*tacchūnyena*). This means "in the absence of the presence of the gem. Now, if [the fire] in the fire...
If it is asked, "Since there is a power conducive to burning, why does burning not occur when a jewel or similar object is present?", he says: "In that case... (tatra).
